passage: Monday: Tenzin handed over his maths test at the dinner table. His mother Binita read the mark and her voice rose, "How can you fail again? What have you been doing?" Tenzin went silent and stared at his rice. He felt very small. Tuesday: he didn't speak much at breakfast, and Binita's mouth was still tight. He decided to wait. Thursday: after tea, when the flat was calm and Binita was folding clothes, he said, "Mummy, I want to get better at maths. Can you help me make a plan?" She stopped folding. "Okay," she said in a softer voice. "Let's look at the mistakes together tonight." Tenzin nodded and fetched his pencil.

qa.q: What did Tenzin do while his mother shouted on Monday?
qa.a: He went silent and stared at his rice.

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel when his mother shouted about his mark?
qa.a: Very small, which is why he went quiet instead of answering back.

qa.q: Why was Thursday a better time for Tenzin to talk to his mother?
qa.a: Things had cooled, and the flat was calm, so Tenzin could say he wanted to improve and ask for help with a plan without a fight.

qa.q: How might Binita have felt when she shouted about the test?
qa.a: Probably worried and frustrated about his mark, though the shouting made Tenzin shrink; later she softened once he asked for her help.

grounding: A child goes quiet when a parent shouts about failing, waits for things to cool, then asks for help with a plan.

passage: The last bell had gone and the corridor was noisy with chairs and shoes. Zeenat stayed at her desk with her failed spelling paper, expecting to feel worse than ever. Ms Dilnaz pulled a chair beside her. "Let's look at this together. See here, you wrote 'recieve'? The rule is i before e, except after c." She circled the word gently. Zeenat's eyes prickled. Nobody had ever stayed after school for her. They went through four more words, and Ms Dilnaz asked her to spell them aloud. At the door Ms Dilnaz said, "I think you'll do better on the next one." Zeenat walked home feeling lighter.

qa.q: What word did Zeenat spell wrongly that Ms Dilnaz pointed out?
qa.a: She wrote 'recieve' instead of the correct spelling.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling when her eyes prickled?
qa.a: Touched and cared for, because nobody had ever stayed after school just for her.

qa.q: Why is accepting Ms Dilnaz's help not a weakness for Zeenat?
qa.a: It shows that someone believes she can improve, and going through the mistakes together turns the failed paper into something she can fix. 🙂

qa.q: What might Ms Dilnaz be thinking when she says she thinks Zeenat will do better?
qa.a: She believes Zeenat can improve, and wants her to know it.

grounding: A child failing a test is cared for by a teacher who stays back to explain the mistakes.

passage: The canteen queue was long and the bell was about to ring. Nitin leaned over Varun's shoulder and grabbed the marks slip from his hand. "Twelve out of thirty! Ha, Varun the genius!" A few kids in the queue turned. Varun's cheeks burned and his stomach dropped. For a second he wanted to snatch it back, or shout something worse. Then he took a breath. "Yeah, I need to practise that chapter," he said, reaching for the slip. "One test isn't all of me." Nitin blinked; he'd expected a fight. Varun moved up in the queue. He remembered Nitin's dictation notebook, with red pen all over it, and said nothing more.

qa.q: What did Nitin grab from Varun's hand in the queue?
qa.a: He grabbed the marks slip.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling when his cheeks burned and his stomach dropped?
qa.a: Hurt and embarrassed, and briefly tempted to snatch back the slip or shout something worse.

qa.q: What choice helped Varun handle Nitin's laughing, and why?
qa.a: Taking a breath and answering calmly, then moving up in the queue, worked because it gave Nitin no fight and kept Varun's dignity.

qa.q: How might Nitin have seen Varun's calm reply?
qa.a: He blinked in surprise, since he had expected a fight, and may not have known what to say.

grounding: A child laughed at over his marks feels hurt, answers calmly and remembers the mocker has weak spots too, under time pressure.

passage: Dear diary, I'm Disha, and I got my science test back today. I failed. I sat at my desk with my face hot, hoping nobody would look. At break I went to the corner by the water tank so no one would see me. Then Mehak came. She said, "I didn't do well last unit either. I cried in the toilet. Want to study together?" I nearly cried right there. We made a list of the chapters I missed, and she said we could go through them on Saturday at her house. I still feel sad about the mark, but the sadness is smaller. It's not just my problem now, it's ours.

qa.q: Where did Disha go at break so nobody would see?
qa.a: Disha went to the corner by the water tank.

qa.q: What made Disha nearly cry when Mehak spoke to Disha?
qa.a: Disha felt relief and gratitude at not being alone, since Mehak said she had struggled too and offered to study together.

qa.q: How does studying together change failure for Disha?
qa.a: It turns it from a private shame into a shared problem with a plan, a list of chapters and a Saturday to work on them.

qa.q: Why might Mehak have chosen to tell Disha about crying in the toilet?
qa.a: To show she understands, since she has been in the same place and does not judge.

grounding: A child who failed a test feels less alone when a friend shares her own struggle and offers to study together.

passage: That evening Lokesh sat on the cot outside the house with his failed test on his knee, and the letters swam. He wanted to tear it up. But he brought the buffaloes in, washed his feet, and looked again. The wrong answers were all in the chapter on fractions. "It's the sums, not me," he told the goat. He pulled a stub of charcoal from the stove and drew a small row of boxes on the wall. He would do a few fraction sums every day after the buffaloes. Baljeet, a boy in Class 8 next door, checked them when he passed. A few weeks later, one more sum came out right, and Lokesh ate an extra piece of gur to celebrate. 🙂

qa.q: Where did Lokesh draw the row of boxes?
qa.a: On the wall, with a stub of charcoal.

qa.q: What did Lokesh mean when he told the goat, "It's the sums, not me"?
qa.a: That the mistakes were in the fractions, which he could practise, and did not mean he himself was stupid.

qa.q: What made Lokesh's approach to the failure work?
qa.a: He looked at the wrong answers without hating himself, chose a small daily practice, had Baljeet check his sums, and celebrated a small improvement.

qa.q: How might Baljeet have seen Lokesh's daily practice?
qa.a: Probably as a sign that he was serious, since he checked the sums whenever he passed.

grounding: A child decides to practise a hard chapter every day after failing and celebrates a small improvement.

passage: Monday night: Tanuja lay in bed, staring at the corner of the room where the shadows looked like a tall person. Her heart thumped, and she pulled the blanket over her nose. She snapped at her sister in the morning for no reason. Tuesday: she told Zeenat didi in a small voice. Zeenat didn't laugh. She went to the corner with Tanuja, and they saw it was just a coat on a hook. "It looked scary, though," Zeenat said. That night she plugged a little lamp in. Two weeks later: Tanuja noticed the lamp had been off since Saturday. The corner was just a corner again, and she was asleep before she remembered to check.

qa.q: What did Tanuja and Zeenat find in the corner?
qa.a: They found it was just a coat on a hook.

qa.q: Why did Tanuja snap at her sister in the morning?
qa.a: She was still shaken by her fear from the night before, and it came out as irritation. 🙂

qa.q: What helped Tanuja's fear of the dark fade?
qa.a: Talking about it with Zeenat, checking the corner together, and having a little lamp, and then time.

qa.q: How might Zeenat have seen Tanuja's fear?
qa.a: As real even though there was nothing dangerous, which is why she did not laugh and said the coat looked scary.

grounding: A child scared of the dark imagines things in a corner, and talking and a small light help the fear fade over weeks.

passage: Dear diary, I'm Sonali. Last night I had a nightmare where I was lost in a huge market and nobody could hear me. I woke up with my heart pounding and my pyjamas all sweaty. I called Amma, and she came in and sat beside me on the bed without saying anything at first. Then she said in her calm voice, "You are safe. I am here. It was only a dream." She rubbed my back slowly and my heart slowed down too. This morning I told my brother Saurabh. He said he once dreamed about a giant crab in the bathtub. We laughed. Telling it out loud made it smaller.

qa.q: What did Sonali dream about?
qa.a: Sonali dreamed of being lost in a huge market where nobody could hear.

qa.q: What made Sonali's heart slow down?
qa.a: Amma's calm presence: Amma sat beside Sonali, said Sonali was safe and rubbed Sonali's back slowly.

qa.q: What can Sonali do the next time Sonali wakes frightened?
qa.a: Sonali can call Amma or tell someone what happened, since sharing the fear made it smaller.

qa.q: How might Saurabh have felt when Sonali told him about the nightmare?
qa.a: Understanding, since he shared his own dream about a giant crab, which made them both laugh.

grounding: A child soothed after a nightmare by Amma's calm words learns that shared fear becomes smaller.

passage: Pool note from Mr Darshan, swimming coach. Urmila stood on the edge of the low board today with her arms tight around herself. Her friend Ritu laughed, "Scaredy-cat!" Urmila's face went red, and she looked as if she might cry. Then she said, "Everybody's afraid of something. You won't even touch a lizard." Ritu stopped laughing. I told Urmila she did not have to jump today and that we would start with sitting on the edge with her feet in the water. She did that for ten minutes and looked calmer. I had a quiet word with Ritu about teasing. At the end, Urmila sat next to another girl, not Ritu.

qa.q: What did Ritu call Urmila?
qa.a: She called her a scaredy-cat.

qa.q: How did Urmila feel when Ritu laughed?
qa.a: Stung and close to tears; her face went red, but she found the words to say everybody is afraid of something.

qa.q: What did Mr Darshan do that helped Urmila with her fear?
qa.a: He told her she did not have to jump that day and started with her sitting at the edge with her feet in the water.

qa.q: Why might Ritu have stopped laughing when Urmila mentioned lizards?
qa.a: Probably because she was reminded that she is afraid of something too, and saw that teasing Urmila was unfair.

grounding: A child called a scaredy-cat by a friend answers that everyone fears something, and is supported by her coach.

passage: Noor's palms were wet as she waited behind the curtain at the colony's Diwali show. On the other side, all the neighbours were sitting on plastic chairs. "You can do it," whispered Thomas, her neighbour from the third floor, giving her a thumbs-up. Her poem tumbled out fast, her voice shaking on the first line, but by the last verse it was steady. When the clapping came, her chest felt huge and warm. Afterwards Thomas grinned. "Bet you can't climb up the water tank ladder now." Noor shook her head. "I did a scary thing on purpose. Climbing that is just silly." She walked off, proud, holding her mother's hand.

qa.q: Where did the show take place?
qa.a: At the colony's Diwali show.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling when her chest felt huge and warm?
qa.a: Pride after facing something she had feared, as the clapping came.

qa.q: Why did Noor refuse to climb the water tank ladder?
qa.a: She knew facing a small fear is different from taking a risk with her safety, so she did not need to prove bravery that way.

qa.q: How might Thomas see Noor's performance?
qa.a: Thomas encouraged her and seems impressed, though Thomas then teased with a dare.

grounding: A child performs on stage despite fear and feels proud, without needing to prove bravery through risk.

passage: After school in the corridor by the lockers, an older boy stepped in front of Wei and leaned close. "Give me your snack tomorrow, or you'll be sorry," he said, low and cold. Wei's knees went weak and his throat closed. He couldn't say anything. The boy walked away. Wei stood there feeling small, and part of him didn't want anyone to know. Xin, his desk partner, found him gripping his bag strap. "What happened? You're pale." Wei told her in a whisper. "We have to tell Mr Lim," said Xin. "That's not okay." Wei's eyes stung, but together they walked to the staffroom, and the teacher listened without interrupting.

qa.q: Where did the older boy stop Wei?
qa.a: In the corridor by the lockers.

qa.q: What was Wei feeling in the corridor, and how could you tell?
qa.a: He was terrified: his knees went weak, his throat closed and he could not speak.

qa.q: What did Wei and Xin do that was a smart choice?
qa.a: They went together to tell the teacher, Mr Lim, instead of facing the threat alone.

qa.q: How might Xin see Wei's situation?
qa.a: As something that is not okay and should not be handled alone, so she urged him to tell Mr Lim.

grounding: A child terrified by an older child's threat does not face it alone but tells a teacher.
